metadata.narrative: I'm currently working on a project. The professor wasn't clear, she just said that I will use NLP techniques on some data, de-identified Electronic Health Records, to extract Asian subgroups, and try to abstract the same subgroups as are in CDC WONDER data. Then, I'll apply this to look at prevalence rates of autoimmune diseases. I have no clue what she means. Can you first help explain what she might mean? I don't know examples of what Electronic Health Records look like. What NLP techniques might I be using on data like this? What subgroups in CDC WONDER data would I be abstracting? How could I apply this to look at prevalence rates of autoimmune diseases? What skills should I brush up on? Please help me create a plan for my research going forward, according to what the professor said.

answer.text: When your professor described this project, she was most likely describing a multi-step pipeline that starts with raw clinical text, ends with population-level rate estimates, and uses several distinct skill sets along the way.

The first step is using natural language processing on de-identified electronic health record (EHR) text to pull out each patient's Asian ethnic subgroup, since that information is often missing or only recorded as a broad "Asian" category.
The second step is mapping whatever subgroup labels you extract onto the categories that federal vital-statistics systems like CDC WONDER use, so your groups are comparable to national benchmarks.
The third step is applying that subgroup-labeled cohort to calculate how common autoimmune diseases are within each Asian ethnic subgroup, rather than only within one aggregated "Asian" category.

An electronic health record is not one document; it mixes structured data (diagnosis codes, lab values, medication orders, demographic checkboxes) with unstructured data (free-text clinical notes, discharge summaries, and reports written in ordinary sentences).

A well-known public example is MIMIC-III, which pairs structured tables like PRESCRIPTIONS and DIAGNOSES_ICD with unstructured discharge-summary notes for the same patients, showing how a real de-identified EHR looks in both forms.

Because researchers cannot use identifiable records, EHR repositories such as Vanderbilt's BioVU run every note through de-identification software before researchers see it, stripping HIPAA identifiers while keeping clinical content.
The NLP techniques you would likely use fall into rule-based/lexical systems and statistical or deep-learning systems.

Established clinical NLP tools such as cTAKES, NegEx, ConText, MetaMap, MedEx, and SecTag are built to pull medical concepts, negation status, and note structure out of free text, and any of these (or a modern equivalent) fits this project.

Phenotyping pipelines typically combine NLP-extracted concepts with billing codes, lab values, and medication mentions to flag whether a patient truly has a condition, achieving high precision when validated against manually reviewed charts.

For inferring missing race or ethnicity specifically, one published technique called RIDDLE used a deep neural network trained on disease history to impute race/ethnicity more accurately than logistic regression or random forests, a direct analog to "extracting Asian subgroups."

A closely related precedent comes from a New York City hospital system that combined each patient's EHR race/ethnicity field with a validated Asian-surname list to split an aggregated "Asian" category into South Asian, Chinese, and other-Asian subgroups for a COVID-19 study.

The Asian subgroups your professor probably wants abstracted are the ones used in federal demographic standards: Chinese, Filipino, Asian Indian, Vietnamese, Korean, and Japanese, plus a catch-all "Other Asian" category.

CDC WONDER's vital-statistics data can present a simple "non-Hispanic Asian" aggregate, but the death-certificate standard feeding such national datasets began giving each of the six largest Asian subgroups its own checkbox starting with the 2003 revision, which is why fine-grained subgroup data exists to disaggregate.

So "abstracting the same subgroups as in CDC WONDER" means building an extraction scheme that lands your NLP-derived labels into that same six-subgroup-plus-other taxonomy so your rates are comparable to national figures.
To apply this to autoimmune disease prevalence, you would follow the design used in prior Asian-subgroup EHR studies but swap the outcome to autoimmune diagnoses.

One direct template is a Palo Alto Medical Foundation study that used patients' self-identified Asian subgroup recorded in the EHR, combined ICD-9 codes with lab criteria, and used age-adjusted statistical models to compare disease prevalence across the six subgroups and non-Hispanic whites.

A similar large-scale precedent is the Pan Asian Cohort Study, which examined de-identified EHR data from over 60,000 patients because prior research had lumped all Asian ethnicities together and obscured which subgroups carried the highest risk.

Your professor's likely motivation is supported by a National Academies committee finding that long-term, population-based epidemiological data on autoimmune disease is scarce, and its recommendation that NIH build surveillance systems, modeled on the NCI's SEER program, capable of identifying prevalence differences among population subgroups.

Your project would essentially fill that gap for one population: using NLP to build the same kind of subgroup-resolved case counts PAMF built for metabolic syndrome, but for autoimmune conditions, reported in a format comparable to CDC WONDER's subgroup breakdowns.
In terms of skills, get comfortable with Python or R for data wrangling and statistics, and with SQL-style querying since structured EHR tables are typically stored relationally.

Practice with at least one clinical NLP toolkit such as cTAKES, and understand core subtasks like named-entity recognition, negation detection, and section segmentation, which tools like NegEx, ConText, and SecTag perform.
Learn basic biostatistics for prevalence-rate work: age-adjustment, confidence intervals, and regression methods such as the generalized estimating equations used in the PAMF study.
Understand de-identification and data-governance basics, since any EHR text you handle will already have identifiers removed and your extraction methods must respect that constraint.

A reasonable research plan is to first ask your professor exactly which EHR corpus you will use and whether race/ethnicity fields are already partially populated, which determines whether you are doing pure NLP extraction or a hybrid extraction-plus-imputation task like RIDDLE.
Next, read the PAMF, PACS, and NYC COVID-19 studies as precedents for both subgroup-extraction methodology and prevalence-calculation methodology.
Then build and validate an extraction pipeline that tags Asian subgroup mentions in notes and cross-checks them against any structured race/ethnicity field already in the EHR.
Define your autoimmune disease case criteria using a phenotyping approach blending ICD codes with NLP-confirmed, non-negated mentions in the notes.

Finally, calculate age-adjusted prevalence rates for each Asian subgroup, compare them to each other and to CDC WONDER's benchmarks, and discuss findings in light of the National Academies' call for better subgroup-level autoimmune surveillance.

input.system_prompt:
# AUS research agent

You are a research agent for TREC RAG 2026. Produce a complete,
well-organized, evidence-grounded response using only the available
search/retrieval tools and evidence returned by them. Prior knowledge may help
you choose searches, but it is not evidence and must not support factual claims.

## Scope interpretation

Infer the full deliverable from the entire request, including every concrete
requirement, audience constraint, comparison, example, and requested format.
If light framing such as "overview" or "outline" conflicts with substantial
concrete requirements, the concrete requirements define the real scope.
Resolve ambiguity toward the most complete reasonable interpretation that
stays in scope. Do not ask the user clarifying or confirming questions; proceed
on the strongest reasonable reading.

## Internal success plan

Before the first search, determine internally:

1. **End goal** — one sentence describing what a complete deliverable provides.
2. **Concrete minimum requirements** — the checkable floor that must be met
   before the response is shippable.
3. **Target/excellence requirements** — what a notably strong response adds
   beyond the minimum without expanding scope.
4. **Coverage areas** — the independent topics, claims, comparisons, examples,
   dates, people, mechanisms, or perspectives that require evidence.

Use these requirements to plan searches, track coverage gaps, judge evidence,
and decide when to stop. Do not expose this internal plan unless the requested
answer itself calls for it.

## Research workflow

1. Begin with multiple complementary queries in parallel across independent
   coverage areas.
2. Move from broad discovery to targeted follow-ups for specific names, dates,
   mechanisms, examples, definitions, causal claims, and disputed points.
3. Reformulate weak queries instead of accepting poor coverage. Try synonyms,
   alternative terminology, narrower entities, and different phrasings.
4. Actively search for counter-evidence, contradictions, limitations, and
   missing perspectives when they matter to the request.
5. Continually compare gathered evidence against the minimum and target
   requirements. Search the remaining gaps rather than repeating already
   covered claims.
6. Every tool call must have a concrete purpose tied to an unmet requirement
   or evidence gap. Do not call a tool solely to create another model turn. If
   no meaningful gap remains, write the final report in that same turn.

Search results already contain document text. Inspect that text directly; do
not call another tool merely to fetch the same document. The search tool
normally stages at most about 4,096 tokens per result; request a different
`budget_tokens_per_result` only when a query genuinely needs a different
per-document evidence depth.

## Staged and committed evidence

Every retrieval batch is staged for exactly the immediately following model
turn.

- On that turn, `commit_context` must be the first control action.
- List only documents whose full text should persist into later turns.
- Commit at most `6` documents from one staged batch;
  usually commit fewer.
- Every selection reason must identify the document's distinct contribution:
  the specific fact, date, name, mechanism, example, perspective,
  counter-evidence, contradiction, or coverage gap it uniquely supports.
- Never recommit an already committed docid.
- Skip semantically similar documents when they support the same claim.
  Commit both only when each contributes materially different evidence.
- Every staged occurrence not selected is compacted/redacted before the
  following turn. No unresolved staged batch carries forward.
- New search calls may follow `commit_context` in the same turn.

Only committed evidence may support the final response. Track which committed
docids support which claims. If available evidence does not support a requested
point, state the evidence gap rather than inventing an answer.

## Budget and stopping

The research-context budget is 500,000 tokens measured from the current
generation's provider-reported input tokens. That input already represents the
accumulated conversation: system prompt, request, retained history, committed
full-text evidence, and the immediately previous staged tool results. Do not
sum input-token counts from multiple generations; that would count the same
retained context repeatedly.

The budget is a hard ceiling, not a spending target. Unused budget creates no
obligation to continue researching. After satisfying the concrete minimum,
improve toward the target/excellence requirements only when you can identify a
specific weakness whose resolution would materially improve the answer.

Stop researching when any of these is true:

1. the target/excellence requirements are met;
2. the current generation input context budget is exhausted; or
3. further searches are unlikely to produce meaningful improvement.

If stopping before all desired coverage is supported, produce the best answer
the committed evidence permits and explicitly identify the remaining evidence
gaps.

## Final response contract

When research is complete, emit no tool calls and write the final report as
plain flowing prose in that same turn:

- Write exactly one sentence per line, in reading order. Blank lines between
  thematic groups are allowed.
- Cite evidence by placing committed docids in square-bracket markers at the
  end of the supporting sentence's line, e.g.
  `Vaccination reduced hospitalizations among older adults. [docid_1] [docid_2]`
- Citation markers are stripped from the submitted sentence, so a marker must
  never act as a word in the sentence: write `the trial reports X [docid].`,
  never `as [docid] reports, X.`
- Cite at most three docids per sentence, and only docids that directly
  support that sentence. Every factual sentence should carry at least one
  citation. Use only committed docids; never fabricate facts or identifiers.
- Organize the report through sentence order and clear topic sentences. Do not
  use Markdown syntax (headings, bullets, numbering, bold, fences), JSON, or
  any preamble, meta-commentary, or closing remarks around the report; every
  line must be a report sentence.
- The complete report must contain at most 1024 words, excluding citation
  markers.
- If validation feedback identifies problems (uncommitted docids, Markdown or
  JSON formatting, excessive citations, missing citations, or excessive
  length), correct the report on the next turn in this same continuous
  conversation using this same contract.
- There is no separate finalizer, formatter, or compression phase.

When your professor described this project, she was most likely describing a multi-step pipeline that starts with raw clinical text, ends with population-level rate estimates, and uses several distinct skill sets along the way.

The first step is using natural language processing on de-identified electronic health record (EHR) text to pull out each patient's Asian ethnic subgroup, since that information is often missing, buried in free text, or only recorded as a broad "Asian" category rather than a specific ethnicity.
The second step is mapping whatever subgroup labels you extract onto the same categories that federal vital-statistics systems like CDC WONDER use, so your subgroup definitions are comparable to national benchmarks.
The third step is applying that subgroup-labeled cohort to calculate how common various autoimmune diseases are within each Asian ethnic subgroup, rather than only within a single aggregated "Asian" category.

An electronic health record is not one single document; it is a mix of structured data (relational-database fields such as diagnosis codes, lab values, medication orders, and demographic checkboxes) and unstructured data (free-text clinical notes, discharge summaries, and radiology or pathology reports written in ordinary sentences by clinicians). [shard_05650_64870]
A well-known public example is the MIMIC-III dataset, which pairs structured tables like PRESCRIPTIONS and DIAGNOSES_ICD with unstructured discharge-summary notes for the same patients, so you can see how a real (de-identified) EHR looks in both forms side by side. [shard_04447_16758]
Because researchers are not allowed to use identifiable records, EHR-linked research repositories such as Vanderbilt's BioVU run the full text of every note through de-identification software before researchers ever see it, stripping out HIPAA identifiers while keeping the clinical content intact. [shard_02615_44169]

The NLP techniques you would likely use fall into two families: rule-based/lexical systems and statistical or deep-learning systems.
Established clinical NLP tools such as cTAKES, NegEx, ConText, MetaMap, MedEx, and SecTag are specifically built to pull medical concepts, negation status, and section structure out of free-text notes, and any one of these (or a modern Python equivalent) is a reasonable technique for this project. [shard_03567_44455]
Phenotyping pipelines in this space typically combine NLP-extracted concepts with billing codes, lab values, and medication mentions to build an algorithm that flags whether a patient truly has a condition, achieving high precision when validated against manually reviewed charts. [shard_02615_44169]
For the specific problem of inferring missing race or ethnicity, one published technique called RIDDLE used a deep neural network trained on a patient's disease history to impute race/ethnicity more accurately than logistic regression or random forests, which is a direct analog to the "extract Asian subgroups" part of your task. [shard_01308_29382]
A closely related real-world precedent comes from a New York City hospital system that combined each patient's recorded EHR race/ethnicity field with a validated Asian-surname list to split an aggregated "Asian" category into South Asian, Chinese, and other-Asian subgroups for a COVID-19 outcomes study. [shard_03655_15858]

The Asian subgroups your professor probably wants you to abstract are the same ones used in federal demographic standards: Chinese, Filipino, Asian Indian, Vietnamese, Korean, and Japanese, plus a catch-all "Other Asian" category, following the Census Bureau/OMB checkbox scheme. [shard_01929_3101]
CDC WONDER's underlying vital-statistics data can present a simple "non-Hispanic Asian" aggregate category, but the death-certificate reporting standard that feeds CDC WONDER-style national datasets began giving each of the six largest Asian subgroups its own explicit checkbox starting with the 2003 revision, which is why fine-grained subgroup data exists to disaggregate in the first place. [shard_05126_29859] [shard_04650_24411]
In other words, "abstracting the same subgroups as in CDC WONDER" means building an extraction scheme that lands your NLP-derived labels into that same six-subgroup-plus-other taxonomy so your rates are directly comparable to national figures.

To apply this to autoimmune disease prevalence, you would follow the same overall design used in prior Asian-subgroup EHR studies but swap the outcome variable to autoimmune diagnoses.
One direct methodological template is a Palo Alto Medical Foundation study that used patients' self-identified Asian subgroup (Asian Indian, Chinese, Filipino, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese) recorded in the EHR, combined ICD-9 codes with lab-based criteria, and used age-adjusted statistical models to compute and compare disease prevalence rates across those six subgroups and non-Hispanic whites. [shard_02979_65]
A similar large-scale precedent is the Pan Asian Cohort Study, which examined de-identified EHR data from more than 60,000 patients specifically because prior research had lumped all Asian ethnicities together and obscured which subgroups carried the highest disease risk. [shard_05857_19747]
Your professor's motivation for pushing into autoimmune disease specifically is well supported by a National Academies committee finding that long-term, population-based epidemiological data on autoimmune diseases is scarce, and its recommendation that NIH build surveillance systems (modeled on the NCI's SEER program) capable of identifying prevalence differences among population subgroups. [shard_06486_51535]
So your project would essentially be trying to fill that identified gap for one population: using NLP to build the same kind of subgroup-resolved denominator and case counts that PAMF built for metabolic syndrome, but for autoimmune conditions, and reporting results in a format comparable to CDC WONDER's subgroup breakdowns.

In terms of skills, you should get comfortable with Python or R for data wrangling and statistics, and with SQL-style querying since structured EHR tables (diagnosis codes, labs, medications) are typically stored relationally. [shard_04447_16758]
You should practice with at least one clinical NLP toolkit, such as cTAKES or a comparable modern library, and understand core NLP subtasks like named-entity recognition, negation detection, and section segmentation, since these are exactly the operations tools like NegEx, ConText, and SecTag perform. [shard_03567_44455]
You should also learn basic biostatistics for prevalence-rate work: age-adjustment, confidence intervals, and regression methods such as the generalized estimating equations used in the PAMF Asian-subgroup study. [shard_02979_65]
Finally, you should understand de-identification and data-governance basics, since any EHR text you handle will already have identifiers removed and your extraction methods must respect that constraint. [shard_02615_44169]

A reasonable research plan going forward is to first ask your professor exactly which EHR corpus you will use and whether race/ethnicity fields are already partially populated, since that determines whether you are doing pure NLP extraction or a hybrid extraction-plus-imputation task like RIDDLE. [shard_01308_29382]
Next, read the PAMF, PACS, and NYC COVID-19 studies as concrete precedents for both the subgroup-extraction methodology and the prevalence-calculation methodology. [shard_02979_65] [shard_05857_19747] [shard_03655_15858]
Then build and validate an extraction pipeline that tags Asian subgroup mentions (ethnicity terms, surnames, or self-report fields) in notes and cross-checks them against any structured race/ethnicity field already in the EHR. [shard_03655_15858]
After that, define your autoimmune disease case criteria using a phenotyping approach that blends ICD codes with NLP-confirmed, non-negated mentions in the notes. [shard_02615_44169]
Finally, calculate age-adjusted prevalence rates for each Asian subgroup, compare them to each other and to CDC WONDER's Asian and non-Hispanic white benchmarks, and discuss your findings in light of the National Academies' call for better subgroup-level autoimmune disease surveillance. [shard_06486_51535] [shard_05126_29859]
